# --- OS Accounts (Login with Open Software) ---------------------------------
# Optional when OS_CLOVY_LOCAL_DEV=1. Identity only in the desktop app.
# The App API key (osk_) is server-side only in Clovy API and never belongs
# in this file.
# Staging example:
#   OS_ACCOUNTS_URL=https://os-accounts-portal-staging.up.railway.app
#   OS_ACCOUNTS_API_URL=https://os-accounts-api-staging.up.railway.app
# `make dev-staging` overrides both URLs. Set the staging OS_ACCOUNTS_CLIENT_ID
# (format: ocl_...) here or in the shell for login to work.
# Set OS_CLOVY_DEV_PLAINTEXT_TOKEN_STORE=1 to avoid repeated Keychain prompts in dev.
OS_ACCOUNTS_URL=
OS_ACCOUNTS_API_URL=
# OAuth client id issued by the OS Accounts admin console (format: ocl_...).
# Sent on the /login URL so OS Accounts can identify Clovy.
OS_ACCOUNTS_CLIENT_ID=
# Loopback port for the login redirect. Must match the redirect_uri allowlisted
# at registration: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback (default 8765).
OS_ACCOUNTS_LOOPBACK_PORT=
# Local dev only: set to 1 in debug builds to avoid macOS Keychain prompts.
# Stores OS Accounts access/refresh tokens in src-tauri/target/dev-os-accounts-tokens.json
# (and Google connector tokens in src-tauri/target/dev-google-connector-tokens.json).
OS_CLOVY_DEV_PLAINTEXT_TOKEN_STORE=0

# Released scripts may still provide OS_JUNE_* and JUNE_API_URL. Clovy reads
# those values only when the corresponding canonical variable is unset.

# --- Private connectors (Google) ---------------------------------------------
# Credentials of the Google Cloud "Desktop app" client used by the
# Gmail/Calendar connectors. Google requires both values at its token endpoint.
# A desktop app cannot keep the client secret confidential (it ships in the
# binary), so PKCE still protects the authorization-code exchange and user
# refresh/access tokens remain the actual secrets. Leave either value empty to
# disable connecting accounts (listing still works).
GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=
GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=
=== clovy-api/.env.example
# Clovy API local env. Copy to clovy-api/.env and fill in real values.
# This file lives next to the Clovy API workspace so service-only secrets stay
# isolated from the Tauri client's env at the repo root.
#
# Figment maps CLOVY__SECTION__FIELD env vars onto AppConfig fields. The
# double underscore (__) is the section separator — single underscores in
# field names stay literal (e.g. APP_API_KEY -> app_api_key).
# Existing JUNE__ variables remain lower-precedence compatibility aliases.

# --- Open source local mode -------------------------------------------------
# Enabled by default so a cloned repo can run without OS Accounts or billing.
# Keep the bearer token in sync with OS_CLOVY_LOCAL_DEV_BEARER_TOKEN in the
# root .env file.
#
# WARNING: the default bearer token below is a publicly known placeholder. That
# is safe only while CLOVY__SERVER__HOST stays on loopback (127.0.0.0/8 or ::1).
# If you rebind the server to a non-loopback address, anyone who can reach the
# port can authenticate with this token (local mode also skips metering), and
# Clovy API refuses to start in that combination. Set a random token instead,
# e.g. `openssl rand -hex 32`, and keep it in sync with the root .env.
CLOVY__SERVER__HOST=127.0.0.1
# Clovy refreshes Venice's model catalog in-process at this interval, so new
# upstream models become selectable without restarting the API. Default: 300.
# CLOVY__SERVER__MODEL_CATALOG_REFRESH_SECS=300
CLOVY__LOCAL_DEV__ENABLED=true
CLOVY__LOCAL_DEV__BEARER_TOKEN=local-dev-token
CLOVY__LOCAL_DEV__USER_ID=usr_local_dev

# --- OS Accounts ------------------------------------------------------------
# Optional when CLOVY__LOCAL_DEV__ENABLED=true. Disable local mode and fill
# these in for a connected deployment with token verification and metering.
# Local OS Accounts example: http://127.0.0.1:3000
# Staging example: https://os-accounts-api-staging.up.railway.app
CLOVY__OS_ACCOUNTS__API_URL=

# Per-app secret issued by the OS Accounts admin console. Server-side only.
# Never embed in the desktop binary or the root .env file.
CLOVY__OS_ACCOUNTS__APP_API_KEY=

# Optional service token used only for anonymous P3A aggregate ingestion into
# OS Accounts. Server-side only; OS Accounts stores the SHA-256 hash. When
# unset, P3A ingest is disabled and reports are logged only.
CLOVY__OS_ACCOUNTS__P3A_INGEST_TOKEN=

# Flat credit Hold authorized for every metered action (transcribe, generate,
# dictate). Skips per-request estimation entirely — the duration probe and
# token pre-count are bypassed in favor of this single value. Trades a bigger
# Hold for not needing to support every audio format the helper might produce.
# Default: 250.
# CLOVY__OS_ACCOUNTS__FLAT_ESTIMATE_CREDITS=250

# --- Upstream providers -----------------------------------------------------
# In local mode, Clovy API exposes only models whose provider has a usable
# key. Fill Venice for the default text, dictation, and private transcription
# models. Fill OpenAI only if you want the default OpenAI transcription model.
# To use a compatible provider, set the matching BASE_URL and add pricing
# entries in config.toml for the model ids you want to expose.
CLOVY__UPSTREAMS__OPENAI__API_KEY=
# CLOVY__UPSTREAMS__OPENAI__BASE_URL=https://api.openai.com/v1
CLOVY__UPSTREAMS__VENICE__API_KEY=VENICE_API_KEY_REPLACE_ME
# CLOVY__UPSTREAMS__VENICE__BASE_URL=https://api.venice.ai/api/v1
# OpenSoftware private-router canary: https://api.opensoftware.co/v1

# --- Issue reports ----------------------------------------------------------
# Optional. The destination is fixed in config.toml: the `june` project in the
# `open-software` org on os-platform. Set the bot user's fellow API key to file
# reports as Issues.
# Without it, reports are accepted but logged only.
# CLOVY__ISSUE_REPORTS__OS_PLATFORM_API_KEY=

# --- Clovy Companion -------------------------------------------------------
# Production relay trust metadata requires Postgres. Local development can
# run without it and keeps linked-device state only until restart.
# CLOVY__COMPANION__DATABASE_URL=postgres://...

---
status: accepted
date: 2026-07-22
---

# Replace the embedded Hermes runtime with a June-owned agent harness

## Context

June currently embeds a pinned Hermes checkout, a relocatable CPython runtime,
two mode-specific gateways, a WebSocket control plane, locally patched approval
semantics, and a broad compatibility suite. This let June reach a capable agent
experience quickly, but the runtime now owns behavior central to the product:
sessions, streaming, tool dispatch, approvals, skills, persistence, and
lifecycle events.

That boundary makes ordinary product changes depend on upstream protocol and
configuration behavior. It also adds substantial installer weight, startup
work, idle processes, release signing work, and compatibility maintenance.

## Decision

June will own the agent harness and use the TypeScript OpenAI Agents SDK for the
model and tool loop.

- A signed local TypeScript service runs as one trusted child process and talks
  to the Tauri host over versioned, newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdio.
- The trusted service owns orchestration only. Rust remains the authority for
  secrets, June API access, persistence, tool execution, path validation,
  safety modes, approvals, and artifacts.
- Model requests continue through June API's existing metered Chat Completions
  route. Direct OpenAI credentials and OpenAI-hosted trace export are not part
  of this design.
- June's SQLite database becomes the source of truth for sessions, runs,
  ordered items, interruptions, artifacts, skill settings, and local traces.
- The harness is not placed inside the execution sandbox. Sandboxed file and
  command capabilities are tools implemented by the trusted host. On macOS,
  command execution keeps the Seatbelt write-jail. On Windows, host file tools
  enforce workspace roots and sandboxed shell execution is unavailable until a
  real operating-system isolation boundary exists.
- Existing Hermes sessions are imported once from the preserved read-only
  state database. The old Hermes home remains recovery data but is never
  started or read by the new runtime after a successful import.
- The production cutover is atomic. June does not ship a Hermes fallback or a
  dual-runtime feature flag.

This decision supersedes ADR-0006, ADR-0009, ADR-0011, ADR-0025, and ADR-0029.
ADR-0018, ADR-0027, ADR-0028, ADR-0031, and ADR-0032 remain binding at the June
product boundary and are reimplemented against the June-owned runtime.

## Consequences

- June can change agent instructions, tools, state, approvals, and presentation
  without waiting for or patching Hermes.
- The desktop bundle no longer carries Hermes, CPython, its dashboard, or its
  compatibility patch set. Release jobs instead build and sign a Node 24
  single-executable service for each desktop target.
- The stdio protocol and persisted item schema become load-bearing June-owned
  contracts. Both are versioned and covered by fixture tests.
- The cutover restores June-owned routines, branching, live steering, manual
  compaction, and run usage. A live instruction is injected at the next model
  boundary and persisted as visible history; if the active run settles before
  consuming it, June submits it as the next turn instead. Messaging channels,
  background delegation, and raw Hermes runtime debugging remain intentionally
  retired. Browser use, Computer use, private connectors, project memory,
  profiles, attachments, and generated media remain June capabilities and
  continue through Rust-owned tools.
- Performance is an acceptance criterion rather than an assumption. The PR
  records before-and-after installer size, runtime-ready latency, idle memory,
  send acknowledgement, first visible stream event, cancellation latency, and
  time to first model token.

## Cutover baseline

The first local release build on an Apple Silicon Mac establishes the following
baseline for the new sidecar. These measurements are not presented as a Hermes
comparison because the old and new runtimes were not measured under an
equivalent harness.

- Node 24 single executable: 120,790,720 bytes
- Sidecar resident memory after initialization: 98,762,752 bytes
- Process spawn to initialized response: 74.02 ms
- Initialization request round trip: 72.47 ms
- First protocol frame: 73.93 ms
- Graceful shutdown request round trip: 0.27 ms
- Complete smoke-test process lifetime: 78.12 ms
- Unsigned local macOS application bundle: 160 MB

The benchmark is reproducible with `pnpm agent-runtime:benchmark` after the
sidecar has been built. Release CI separately verifies signing, checksums,
startup from a path containing spaces, and the absence of Hermes or Python
payloads.

## Alternatives considered

- Continue patching and upgrading Hermes. Rejected because it preserves the
  product-iteration and packaging costs that motivated the change.
- Run the harness in June API. Rejected because local files, private
  connectors, approvals, and execution should remain on the user's device.
- Run the Agents SDK in the webview. Rejected because the webview must not own
  service credentials, unrestricted tools, or persistence authority.
- Implement the entire agent loop in Rust. Rejected because it would duplicate
  a maintained SDK while adding a slower path to feature parity.

messages.text:
O agente de IA do Clovy é um harness próprio escrito em TypeScript sobre o **OpenAI Agents SDK** (`@openai/agents` 0.13.3). Ele roda como um processo Node separado ao lado do app e conversa com o Rust por stdio. A decisão está no [ADR-0038](docs/adr/0038-june-owned-openai-agents-runtime.md), que substituiu o antigo runtime embutido (Hermes, em Python).

A regra central: **o sidecar TypeScript só orquestra o loop do modelo. O Rust é a autoridade** sobre segredos, acesso à API, persistência, execução de ferramentas, validação de caminhos, sandbox e aprovações.

## As 4 camadas

```
React (webview)  ──Tauri commands──▶  Rust host (src-tauri)  ──stdio JSON-RPC──▶  Sidecar Node (agent-runtime)
      ▲                                  │    ▲                                        │
      └──── evento clovy://agent-runtime-event ┘    └──── tool.invoke (ferramentas + chamada ao modelo) ◀─┘
                                         │
                                         ├──▶ SQLite local (sessões, runs, itens, artefatos)
                                         └──▶ Clovy API /v1/chat/completions ──▶ Venice / OpenAI
```

### 1. Sidecar: [`agent-runtime/`](agent-runtime/)

Cerca de 2 mil linhas de TypeScript.
- **Loop do agente:** [`sdk-engine.ts`](agent-runtime/src/sdk-engine.ts) roda o Agents SDK, com streaming, tool calls, raciocínio e steering.
- **Serviço e transporte:** [`service.ts`](agent-runtime/src/service.ts) e [`transport.ts`](agent-runtime/src/transport.ts) servem JSON-RPC 2.0 delimitado por linha no stdin/stdout.
- **Protocolo versionado:** [`protocol.ts`](agent-runtime/src/protocol.ts) define três grupos de métodos.
  - Host → sidecar: `runtime.initialize`, `run.start`, `run.steer`, `run.cancel`, `run.resume`, `history.compact`, `runtime.shutdown`.
  - Sidecar → host: `tool.invoke` e `host.log`.
  - Eventos: `message.delta`, `reasoning.delta`, `tool.started/completed/failed`, `interruption.requested` (aprovação), `usage.updated`, `run.completed/cancelled/failed`.
- **Como o modelo é chamado:** o sidecar **não chama o modelo direto**. messages.text:
Sim, o harness é o OpenAI Agents SDK (`@openai/agents` 0.13.3). O único outro pacote de runtime do sidecar é o `zod` (veja [`agent-runtime/package.json`](agent-runtime/package.json)). Não tem Pi, Claude Agent SDK nem Codex como motor do agente.

Mesmo sendo o SDK da OpenAI, o modelo não é necessariamente da OpenAI. O SDK usa o adaptador genérico de Chat Completions (`OpenAIChatCompletionsModel`), e a chamada sai pelo Rust para a Clovy API, que roteia para a Venice (ou a OpenAI, se configurada). Na prática, o SDK serve só como motor do loop: ferramentas, streaming e interrupções.

Onde Claude Code e Codex aparecem no código:

- **Como CLIs externas, não como runtime.** O agente do Clovy pode rodar `claude`, `codex`, `gemini` ou `opencode` pela ferramenta `run_shell`, como qualquer outro comando.
  - Existe uma configuração "Agent CLI access" ([`src/lib/agent-cli-access.ts`](src/lib/agent-cli-access.ts)) que, com sua aprovação, libera escrita nas pastas de estado dessas CLIs dentro do sandbox. Sem isso elas não conseguem manter login nem salvar estado.
  - Nesse caso o Clovy só chama o binário instalado na sua máquina; não há integração de protocolo.
- **Importação de projetos do Claude:** um diálogo que importa projetos para as pastas do Clovy ([`ImportClaudeProjectsDialog.tsx`](src/components/folders/ImportClaudeProjectsDialog.tsx)). Não tem relação com o runtime.
- **Menções soltas:** um comentário de estilo em `AppSettings.tsx` e uma lista de apps em `computer_use.rs`.

Trocar o motor por Claude Agent SDK, Pi ou Codex seria viável. A fronteira é o protocolo stdio versionado ([`protocol.ts`](agent-runtime/src/protocol.ts)), e as ferramentas, a persistência e as aprovações ficam todas no Rust. Seria preciso reescrever basicamente o `sdk-engine.ts` e o `rpc-model-provider.ts`, mantendo o mesmo contrato. Pelas regras do repo, isso também exigiria um novo ADR substituindo o 0038.

input.description: Research Pi agent framework API
input.prompt:
Research the current state (as of late September 2026) of "Pi", the TypeScript agent toolkit by Mario Zechner (GitHub monorepo badlogic/pi-mono; npm packages under @mariozechner/ such as pi-ai, pi-agent-core, pi-coding-agent). I am evaluating replacing the OpenAI Agents SDK (@openai/agents) as the agent-loop engine inside a Node 24 sidecar process. Use web search/fetch on the GitHub repo, READMEs, source, and npm. Report concrete, cited facts only; mark anything you could not verify.

Answer each of these precisely:
1. Package layout: which package provides the agent loop (vs LLM abstraction vs coding-agent CLI)? Latest versions, license, release cadence, Node version requirement, runtime dependencies (count/weight), ESM/CJS, whether it bundles cleanly with esbuild into a single CJS file for a Node SEA (single executable application).
2. LLM layer (pi-ai): how providers are defined; can I plug a CUSTOM transport where every model request is sent through my own function (e.g. an RPC to a host process) instead of pi making HTTP calls itself? Is there an OpenAI Chat Completions compatible provider with a configurable baseURL/headers/custom fetch? Streaming event shape (text deltas, reasoning/thinking deltas, tool call deltas, usage/cost). How reasoning fields (`reasoning`, `reasoning_content`) from OpenAI-compatible providers such as Venice are handled.
3. Agent loop (pi-agent-core or equivalent): API to run a turn; message/history format and whether I own persistence (can I supply/serialize the full transcript myself, resume from stored state); tool definition format (TypeBox? zod? JSON schema?); how tool execution works (can tool execution be delegated to an async function that does an RPC and may take minutes); parallel tool calls; abort/cancellation via AbortSignal; events emitted (list them); support for injecting user messages mid-run ("steering" / "follow-up" queues); human-in-the-loop approval / interruption of a tool call and resuming later (possibly after process restart); context compaction/summarization support; usage accounting.
4. Maturity and risk: stars, contributors, breaking-change frequency, notable users, docs quality, issues about stability. Is the agent-core API documented as stable?
5. Anything that makes Pi a poor fit for a desktop app sidecar where the host (Rust) owns all tools, secrets, model HTTP calls, and persistence.

Return a structured report under 900 words with source URLs inline.

messages.content:
1	# @earendil-works/pi-agent-core
2	
3	Stateful agent with tool execution and event streaming. Built on `@earendil-works/pi-ai`.
4	
5	## Installation
6	
7	```bash
8	npm install @earendil-works/pi-agent-core
9	```
10	
11	### SQLite session backends
12	
13	The SQLite session backend and the `node:sqlite` adapter live in a separate package, `@earendil-works/pi-session-backend-sqlite-node`, so the core package does not pull in runtime builtins or native SQLite dependencies by default. The backend accepts a runtime-specific SQLite factory, allowing other session backends to ship as their own packages in the future.
14	
15	## Quick Start
16	
17	```typescript
18	import { Agent } from "@earendil-works/pi-agent-core";
19	import { createModels } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai";
20	import { anthropicProvider } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/providers/anthropic";
21	
22	const models = createModels();
23	models.setProvider(anthropicProvider());
24	const model = models.getModel("anthropic", "claude-sonnet-4-6");
25	if (!model) throw new Error("Model not found");
26	
27	const agent = new Agent({
28	  initialState: {
29	    systemPrompt: "You are a helpful assistant.",
30	    model,
31	  },
32	  streamFn: models.streamSimple.bind(models),
33	});
34	
35	agent.subscribe((event) => {
36	  if (event.type === "message_update" && event.assistantMessageEvent.type === "text_delta") {
37	    // Stream just the new text chunk
38	    process.stdout.write(event.assistantMessageEvent.delta);
39	  }
40	});
41	
42	await agent.prompt("Hello!");
43	```
44	
45	## Experimental facet services
46	
47	Transport-neutral facet-service primitives live in `@earendil-works/chord`. The agent core does not export the service runtime.
48	
49	## Core Concepts
50	
51	### AgentMessage vs LLM Message
52	
53	The agent works with `AgentMessage`, a flexible type that can include:
54	- Standard LLM messages (`user`, `assistant`, `toolResult`)
55	- Custom app-specific message types via declaration merging
56	
57	LLMs only understand `user`, `assistant`, and `toolResult`. The `convertToLlm` function bridges this gap by filtering and transforming messages before each LLM call.
58	
59	### Message Flow
60	
61	```
62	AgentMessage[] → transformContext() → AgentMessage[] → convertToLlm() → Message[] → LLM
63	                    (optional)                           (required)
64	```
65	
66	1. **transformContext**: Prune old messages, inject external context
67	2. **convertToLlm**: Filter out UI-only messages, convert custom types to LLM format
68	
69	## Event Flow
70	
71	The agent emits events for UI updates. Understanding the event sequence helps build responsive interfaces.
72	
73	### prompt() Event Sequence
74	
75	When you call `prompt("Hello")`:
76	
77	```
78	prompt("Hello")
79	├─ agent_start
80	├─ turn_start
81	├─ message_start   { message: userMessage }      // Your prompt
82	├─ message_end     { message: userMessage }
83	├─ message_start   { message: assistantMessage } // LLM starts responding
84	├─ message_update  { message: partial... }       // Streaming chunks
85	├─ message_update  { message: partial... }
86	├─ message_end     { message: assistantMessage } // Complete response
87	├─ turn_end        { message, toolResults: [] }
88	└─ agent_end       { messages: [...] }
89	```
90	
91	### With Tool Calls
92	
93	If the assistant calls tools, the loop continues:
94	
95	```
96	prompt("Read config.json")
97	├─ agent_start
98	├─ turn_start
99	├─ message_start/end  { userMessage }
100	├─ message_start      { assistantMessage with toolCall }
101	├─ message_update...
102	├─ message_end        { assistantMessage }
103	├─ tool_execution_start  { toolCallId, toolName, args }
104	├─ tool_execution_update { partialResult }           // If tool streams
105	├─ tool_execution_end    { toolCallId, result }
106	├─ message_start/end  { toolResultMessage }
107	├─ turn_end           { message, toolResults: [toolResult] }
108	│
109	├─ turn_start                                        // Next turn
110	├─ message_start      { assistantMessage }           // LLM responds to tool result
111	├─ message_update...
112	├─ message_end
113	├─ turn_end
114	└─ agent_end
115	```
116	
117	Tool execution mode is configurable:
118	
119	- `parallel` (default): preflight tool calls sequentially, execute allowed tools concurrently, emit `tool_execution_end` as soon as each tool is finalized, then emit toolResult messages and `turn_end.toolResults` in assistant source order
120	- `sequential`: execute tool calls one by one, matching the historical behavior
121	
122	In parallel mode, tool completion events follow tool completion order, but persisted toolResult messages still follow assistant source order.
123	
124	The mode can be set globally via `toolExecution` in the agent config, or per-tool via `executionMode` on `AgentTool`. If any tool call in a batch targets a tool with `executionMode: "sequential"`, the entire batch executes sequentially regardless of the global setting.
125	
126	The `beforeToolCall` hook runs after `tool_execution_start` and validated argument parsing. It can block execution and attach `terminate: true` to the blocked result. The `afterToolCall` hook runs after tool execution finishes and before `tool_execution_end` and final tool result message events are emitted.
127	
128	Tools, blocked `beforeToolCall` results, and `afterToolCall` overrides can return `terminate: true` to hint that the automatic follow-up LLM call should be skipped. The loop only stops early when every finalized tool result in that batch sets `terminate: true`. Mixed batches continue normally.
129	
130	When you use the `Agent` class, assistant `message_end` processing is treated as a barrier before tool preflight begins. That means `beforeToolCall` sees agent state that already includes the assistant message that requested the tool call.
131	
132	### Request preparation and turn finalization
133	
134	`prepareRequest` runs immediately before every conversational provider request, including the first. Use it to install canonical persisted context after pending input has been emitted:
135	
136	```typescript
137	agent.prepareRequest = async ({ context }) => ({
138	  context: { ...context, messages: await session.loadModelContext() },
139	});
140	```
141	
142	`prepareRequest` does not poll queues. Steering queued while it runs waits for the next normal steering poll.
143	
144	`finishTurn` runs after the assistant and all tool results are finalized, but before `turn_end`. It runs for normal, error, and aborted responses:
145	
146	```typescript
147	agent.finishTurn = async ({ message }) => {
148	  if (message.stopReason === "error" || message.stopReason === "aborted") return;
149	  if (shouldEndRun(message)) return { action: "end" };
150	  return needsAnotherResponse(message) ? { action: "continue" } : undefined;
151	};
152	```
153	
154	Returning `undefined` preserves normal scheduling. `{ action: "end" }` stops immediately after `turn_end`, before polling steering or follow-up queues or preparing another request. On a normal response, `{ action: "continue" }` ensures one next provider request. If tool results, steering, or a follow-up already cause that request, they satisfy the decision and no additional request is made; otherwise the loop makes one context-only request. Error and aborted responses remain hard exits, so their decisions are ignored. `finishTurn` runs again after the next request, so returning `{ action: "continue" }` unconditionally creates an endless loop.
155	
156	To migrate from the removed `shouldStopAfterTurn`, return `{ action: "end" }`. Guard error and aborted responses to preserve the old hook's normal-response-only invocation, especially when the predicate has side effects or assumes a successful response:
157	
158	```typescript
159	finishTurn: async (turn, signal) => {
160	  if (turn.message.stopReason === "error" || turn.message.stopReason === "aborted") return;
161	  return (await shouldStop(turn, signal)) ? { action: "end" } : undefined;
162	},
163	```
164	
165	Each provider turn follows this lifecycle:
166	
167	```text
168	selected input events
169	→ prepareRequest
170	→ provider response
171	→ tool results
172	→ finishTurn
173	→ turn_end
174	→ existing continuation scheduling or agent_end
175	```
176	
177	### continue() and queued input
178	
179	`continue()` retains its existing queue behavior. Empty and system-only transcripts reject without consuming queues. A non-assistant tail continues from existing context: steering is polled at startup, while follow-up input waits until the response naturally stops.
180	
181	```typescript
182	agent.followUp({ role: "user", content: "After the retry", timestamp: Date.now() });
183	await agent.continue(); // The first request retries the existing user/toolResult tail.
184	```
185	
186	An assistant tail cannot be sent directly, so `continue()` falls back to one queued steering batch, then one queued follow-up batch. Queue mode still controls whether that selected batch contains one message or all messages:
187	
188	```typescript
189	agent.steer({ role: "user", content: "Continue from here", timestamp: Date.now() });
190	await agent.continue(); // Uses the queued message only because the tail is assistant.
191	```
192	
193	### Event Types
194	
195	| Event | Description |
196	|-------|-------------|
197	| `agent_start` | Agent begins processing |
198	| `agent_end` | Final event for the run. Awaited subscribers for this event still count toward settlement |
199	| `turn_start` | New turn begins (one LLM call + tool executions) |
200	| `turn_end` | Turn completes with assistant message and tool results |
201	| `message_start` | Any message begins (user, assistant, toolResult) |
202	| `message_update` | **Assistant only.** Includes `assistantMessageEvent` with delta |
203	| `message_end` | Message completes |
204	| `tool_execution_start` | Tool begins |
205	| `tool_execution_update` | Tool streams progress |
206	| `tool_execution_end` | Tool completes |
207	
208	`Agent.subscribe()` listeners are awaited in registration order. `agent_end` means no more loop events will be emitted, but `await agent.waitForIdle()` and `await agent.prompt(...)` only settle after awaited `agent_end` listeners finish.
209	
210	## Agent Options
211	
212	```typescript
213	const agent = new Agent({
214	  // Initial state. systemPrompt and tools become the leading system message
215	  // unless messages already starts with one.
216	  initialState: {
217	    systemPrompt: string,
218	    model: Model<any>,
219	    thinkingLevel: "off" | "minimal" | "low" | "medium" | "high" | "xhigh" | "max",
220	    tools: AgentTool<any>[],
221	    messages: AgentMessage[],
222	  },
223	
224	  // Convert AgentMessage[] to LLM Message[] (required for custom message types)
225	  convertToLlm: (messages) => messages.filter(...),
226	
227	  // Transform context before convertToLlm (for pruning, compaction)
228	  transformContext: async (messages, signal) => pruneOldMessages(messages),
229	
230	  // Steering mode: "one-at-a-time" (default) or "all"
231	  steeringMode: "one-at-a-time",
232	
233	  // Follow-up mode: "one-at-a-time" (default) or "all"
234	  followUpMode: "one-at-a-time",
235	
236	  // Required stream function. Receives a TranscriptContext: the prompt and tools
237	  // are in the transcript's system messages, not on the context.
238	  streamFn: models.streamSimple.bind(models),
239	
240	  // Session ID for provider caching
241	  sessionId: "session-123",
242	
243	  // Dynamic API key resolution (for expiring OAuth tokens)
244	  getApiKey: async (provider) => refreshToken(),
245	
246	  // Tool execution mode: "parallel" (default) or "sequential"
247	  toolExecution: "parallel",
248	
249	  // Preflight each tool call after args are validated. Can block execution.
250	  beforeToolCall: async ({ toolCall, args, context }) => {
251	    if (toolCall.name === "bash") {
252	      return { block: true, reason: "bash is disabled", terminate: true };
253	    }
254	  },
255	
256	  // Postprocess each tool result before final tool events are emitted.
257	  afterToolCall: async ({ toolCall, result, isError, context }) => {
258	    if (toolCall.name === "notify_done" && !isError) {
259	      return { terminate: true };
260	    }
261	    if (!isError) {
262	      return { details: { ...result.details, audited: true } };
263	    }
264	  },
265	
266	  // Rebuild finalized context immediately before every provider request.
267	  prepareRequest: async ({ context }, signal) => {
268	    return { context: { ...context, messages: await loadCanonicalMessages(signal) } };
269	  },
270	
271	  // Finalize a completed turn before turn_end is emitted.
272	  // `continue` ensures one next request; existing tool/queue scheduling can satisfy it.
273	  // `end` ends this run after turn_end without polling queues.
274	  finishTurn: async ({ message, toolResults }, signal) => {
275	    return shouldContinue(message, toolResults) ? { action: "continue" } : undefined;
276	  },
277	
278	  // Custom thinking budgets for token-based providers
279	  thinkingBudgets: {
280	    minimal: 128,
281	    low: 512,
282	    medium: 1024,
283	    high: 2048,
284	  },
285	});
286	```
287	
288	## Agent State
289	
290	```typescript
291	interface AgentState {
292	  model: Model<any>;
293	  thinkingLevel: ThinkingLevel;
294	  tools: AgentTool<any>[];
295	  messages: AgentMessage[];
296	  readonly isStreaming: boolean;
297	  readonly streamingMessage?: AgentMessage;
298	  readonly pendingToolCalls: ReadonlySet<string>;
299	  readonly errorMessage?: string;
300	}
301	```
302	
303	Access state via `agent.state`.
304	
305	Assigning `agent.state.tools = [...]` or `agent.state.messages = [...]` copies the top-level array before storing it. Mutating the returned array mutates the current agent state.
306	
307	The transcript owns the system prompt and tool declarations: the leading system message is the prompt, later system messages patch it (see `SystemMessage` in pi-ai). `agent.state.systemPrompt` is read-only and replays the transcript. `agent.state.tools` is the executable loadout; before every request the loop diffs it against the tools the transcript declares and, if they differ, announces the change in a system message (merged into a pending system message when one exists). pi-ai's `getCurrentSystemMessage(messages)` returns the replayed head, including declared tools, for any message array, including agent transcripts with custom message roles.
308	
309	To change the prompt mid-conversation, append a system message with `content` (added instructions) or `sections` (named replacements):
310	
311	```typescript
312	await agent.prompt([
313	  { role: "system", content: "", sections: { skills: "<skills>...</skills>" }, timestamp: Date.now() },
314	  { role: "user", content: "Continue", timestamp: Date.now() },
315	]);
316	```
317	
318	During streaming, `agent.state.streamingMessage` contains the current partial assistant message.
319	
320	`agent.state.isStreaming` remains `true` until the run fully settles, including awaited `agent_end` subscribers.
321	
322	## Methods
323	
324	### Prompting
325	
326	```typescript
327	// Text prompt
328	await agent.prompt("Hello");
329	
330	// With images
331	await agent.prompt("What's in this image?", [
332	  { type: "image", data: base64Data, mimeType: "image/jpeg" }
333	]);
334	
335	// AgentMessage directly
336	await agent.prompt({ role: "user", content: "Hello", timestamp: Date.now() });
337	
338	// Continue existing non-assistant input; an assistant tail may use queued input as fallback
339	await agent.continue();
340	```
341	
342	### State Management
343	
344	```typescript
345	agent.state.model = getModel("openai", "gpt-4o");
346	agent.state.thinkingLevel = "medium";
347	agent.state.tools = [myTool];
348	agent.toolExecution = "sequential";
349	agent.beforeToolCall = async ({ toolCall }) => undefined;
350	agent.afterToolCall = async ({ toolCall, result }) => undefined;
351	agent.prepareRequest = async ({ context }) => ({
352	  context: { ...context, messages: await loadCanonicalMessages() },
353	});
354	agent.finishTurn = async () => undefined;
355	agent.state.messages = newMessages; // top-level array is copied
356	agent.state.messages.push(message);
357	const nextQueuedMessages = agent.peekQueuedMessages(); // respects queue modes; does not consume
358	agent.reset();
359	```
360	
361	### Session and Thinking Budgets
362	
363	```typescript
364	agent.sessionId = "session-123";
365	
366	agent.thinkingBudgets = {
367	  minimal: 128,
368	  low: 512,
369	  medium: 1024,
370	  high: 2048,
371	};
372	```
373	
374	### Control
375	
376	```typescript
377	agent.abort();           // Cancel current operation
378	await agent.waitForIdle(); // Wait for completion
379	```
380	
381	### Events
382	
383	```typescript
384	const unsubscribe = agent.subscribe(async (event, signal) => {
385	  if (event.type === "agent_end") {
386	    // Final barrier work for the run
387	    await flushSessionState(signal);
388	  }
389	});
390	unsubscribe();
391	```
392	
393	## Steering and Follow-up
394	
395	Steering messages let you interrupt the agent while tools are running. Follow-up messages let you queue work after the agent would otherwise stop.
396	
397	```typescript
398	agent.steeringMode = "one-at-a-time";
399	agent.followUpMode = "one-at-a-time";
400	
401	// While agent is running tools
402	agent.steer({
403	  role: "user",
404	  content: "Stop! Do this instead.",
405	  timestamp: Date.now(),
406	});
407	
408	// After the agent finishes its current work
409	agent.followUp({
410	  role: "user",
411	  content: "Also summarize the result.",
412	  timestamp: Date.now(),
413	});
414	
415	const steeringMode = agent.steeringMode;
416	const followUpMode = agent.followUpMode;
417	
418	agent.clearSteeringQueue();
419	agent.clearFollowUpQueue();
420	agent.clearAllQueues();
421	```
422	
423	Use clearSteeringQueue, clearFollowUpQueue, or clearAllQueues to drop queued messages.
424	
425	When steering messages are detected after a turn completes:
426	1. All tool calls from the current assistant message have already finished
427	2. Steering messages are injected
428	3. The LLM responds on the next turn
429	
430	Follow-up messages are checked only when there are no more tool calls and no steering messages. If any are queued, they are injected and another turn runs.
431	
432	## Custom Message Types
433	
434	Extend `AgentMessage` via declaration merging:
435	
436	```typescript
437	declare module "@earendil-works/pi-agent-core" {
438	  interface CustomAgentMessages {
439	    notification: { role: "notification"; text: string; timestamp: number };
440	  }
441	}
442	
443	// Now valid
444	const msg: AgentMessage = { role: "notification", text: "Info", timestamp: Date.now() };
445	```
446	
447	Handle custom types in `convertToLlm`:
448	
449	```typescript
450	const agent = new Agent({
451	  streamFn: models.streamSimple.bind(models),
452	  convertToLlm: (messages) => messages.flatMap(m => {
453	    if (m.role === "notification") return []; // Filter out
454	    return [m];
455	  }),
456	});
457	```
458	
459	## Tools
460	
461	Define tools using `AgentTool`:
462	
463	```typescript
464	import { Type } from "typebox";
465	
466	const readFileTool: AgentTool = {
467	  name: "read_file",
468	  label: "Read File",  // For UI display
469	  description: "Read a file's contents",
470	  parameters: Type.Object({
471	    path: Type.String({ description: "File path" }),
472	  }),
473	  // Override execution mode for this tool (optional).
474	  // "sequential" forces the entire batch to run one at a time.
475	  // "parallel" allows concurrent execution with other tool calls.
476	  // If omitted, the global toolExecution config applies.
477	  executionMode: "sequential",
478	  execute: async (toolCallId, params, signal, onUpdate) => {
479	    const content = await fs.readFile(params.path, "utf-8");
480	
481	    // Optional: stream progress
482	    onUpdate?.({ content: [{ type: "text", text: "Reading..." }], details: {} });
483	
484	    // Optional: add `terminate: true` here to skip the automatic follow-up LLM call
485	    // when every finalized tool result in the batch does the same.
486	    return {
487	      content: [{ type: "text", text: content }],
488	      details: { path: params.path, size: content.length },
489	    };
490	  },
491	};
492	
493	agent.state.tools = [readFileTool];
494	```
495	
496	### Error Handling
497	
498	**Throw an error** when a tool fails. Do not return error messages as content.
499	
500	```typescript
501	execute: async (toolCallId, params, signal, onUpdate) => {
502	  if (!fs.existsSync(params.path)) {
503	    throw new Error(`File not found: ${params.path}`);
504	  }
505	  // Return content only on success
506	  return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "..." }] };
507	}
508	```
509	
510	Thrown errors are caught by the agent and reported to the LLM as tool errors with `isError: true`.
511	
512	Return `terminate: true` from `execute()`, a blocked `beforeToolCall`, or `afterToolCall` to hint that the agent should stop after the current tool batch. This only takes effect when every finalized tool result in the batch is terminating. The hint is runtime-only; emitted `toolResult` transcript messages remain standard LLM tool results.
513	
514	### MCP and Codemode
515	
516	`@earendil-works/pi-mcp` connects to MCP servers and `@earendil-works/pi-codemode` runs model-written JavaScript that calls tools. [examples/mcp-codemode](examples/mcp-codemode) wraps both as `AgentTool`s: one tool per MCP tool, and a `codemode` tool whose scripts call the agent's tools through `runToolCall()`, so `beforeToolCall` and `afterToolCall` apply to those calls too.
517	
518	## Proxy Usage
519	
520	For browser apps that proxy through a backend:
521	
522	```typescript
523	import { Agent, streamProxy } from "@earendil-works/pi-agent-core";
524	
525	const agent = new Agent({
526	  streamFn: (model, context, options) =>
527	    streamProxy(model, context, {
528	      ...options,
529	      authToken: "...",
530	      proxyUrl: "https://your-server.com",
531	    }),
532	});
533	```
534	
535	## Low-Level API
536	
537	For direct control without the Agent class:
538	
539	```typescript
540	import { agentLoop, agentLoopContinue } from "@earendil-works/pi-agent-core";
541	
542	const context: AgentContext = {
543	  messages: [{ role: "system", content: "You are helpful.", timestamp: Date.now() }],
544	  tools: [],
545	};
546	
547	const config: AgentLoopConfig = {
548	  model: getModel("openai", "gpt-4o"),
549	  convertToLlm: (msgs) => msgs.filter(m => ["user", "assistant", "toolResult"].includes(m.role)),
550	  toolExecution: "parallel",  // overridden by per-tool executionMode if set
551	  beforeToolCall: async ({ toolCall, args, context }) => undefined,
552	  afterToolCall: async ({ toolCall, result, isError, context }) => undefined,
553	};
554	
555	const userMessage = { role: "user", content: "Hello", timestamp: Date.now() };
556	
557	const streamFn = models.streamSimple.bind(models);
558	for await (const event of agentLoop([userMessage], context, config, undefined, streamFn)) {
559	  console.log(event.type);
560	}
561	
562	// Continue from existing context
563	for await (const event of agentLoopContinue(context, config, undefined, streamFn)) {
564	  console.log(event.type);
565	}
566	```
567	
568	These low-level streams are observational. They preserve event order, but they do not wait for your async event handling to settle before later producer phases continue. If you need message processing to act as a barrier before tool preflight, use the `Agent` class instead of raw `agentLoop()` or `agentLoopContinue()`.
569	
570	## License
571	
572	MIT
573

messages.content:
# @earendil-works/pi-durable

> **Experimental.** The API changes without notice between releases.

A durable agent harness. Conversations, model turns, tool calls, and your own state are committed to storage before anything is shown. If the process dies mid-turn, reopening the storage picks the work up where it stopped.

Built on [`@earendil-works/pi-ai`](../ai/README.md) for model access and `@earendil-works/chord` for document state.

## Table of Contents

- [Installation](#installation)
- [Quick Start](#quick-start)
- [Concepts](#concepts)
- [Persist and Resume](#persist-and-resume)
- [Tools](#tools)
- [System Prompt](#system-prompt)
- [Conversation Settings](#conversation-settings)
- [Watching a Conversation](#watching-a-conversation)
- [Busy Conversations](#busy-conversations)
- [Reset and Handoff](#reset-and-handoff)
- [Agent Events (Experimental)](#agent-events-experimental)
- [Hooks](#hooks)
- [More Conversations and Forks](#more-conversations-and-forks)
- [Abort and Subagents](#abort-and-subagents)
- [Your Own State](#your-own-state)
- [Usage and Cost](#usage-and-cost)
- [Storage](#storage)
- [Examples](#examples)
- [Design Documents](#design-documents)

## Installation

```bash
npm install @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/chord
```

## Quick Start

```typescript
import { BACKGROUND_CONTEXT } from "@earendil-works/chord/context";
import { createModels } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/models";
import { openaiProvider } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai/providers/openai";
import { AssistantEntry, createRegistry, Harness, MemoryStorage } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable";

const context = BACKGROUND_CONTEXT;

const models = createModels();
models.setProvider(openaiProvider()); // reads OPENAI_API_KEY

const harness = await Harness.open(new MemoryStorage(), { models, registry: createRegistry() }, context);
const root = await harness.root(context);
await root.setModel({ provider: "openai", modelId: "gpt-6-sol" }, context);

const submission = await root.submit({ type: "input", content: "What is the capital of France?" }, context);
const settled = await submission.wait(context);
if (settled.status === "done" && settled.type === "input") {
	const answer = await root.commit((tx) => tx.entry(AssistantEntry, settled.answer), context);
	console.log(answer?.model?.[0]);
}
await harness.close(context);
```

What happened:

- `Harness.open()` opens a Session over a storage backend. `MemoryStorage` keeps everything in memory.
- `root()` returns the root conversation, creating it on first use. A conversation is a transcript of immutable entries.
- `submit()` durably admits your input and returns a `Submission`. A built-in generation task calls the model and appends the answer.
- `wait()` resolves once the input is answered (`done`) or has failed (`unanswered`, with a reason).

Every async call takes a Chord `Context`, which carries cancellation. `BACKGROUND_CONTEXT` never cancels. Cancelling a wait only cancels that wait, never the work.

## Concepts

- **Harness**: one open storage plus the machinery that runs agents on it. All changes go through one line of atomic commits, and nothing is shown before its commit is stored.
- **Conversation**: a transcript. `root()` creates the root conversation on first use; you can create more and fork them. A `Conversation` handle holds no state; compare handles by `id`.
- **Entry**: one immutable transcript record, such as a user message (`pi.user`), a model response (`pi.assistant`), a tool result (`pi.tool-result`), a system prompt change (`pi.system`), a reset (`pi.reset`), or your own kind. The model sees the entries from the newest reset onward.
- **Commit**: an atomic write. `conversation.commit((tx) => ...)` can append entries, edit documents, and create tasks together; either all of it is stored or none of it.
- **Document**: typed JSON state stored next to the transcript and changed in commits. Built-in ones hold each conversation's settings (`pi.conversation.config`), the running generation and tools (`pi.live`), queued submissions (`pi.inbox`), and spend (`pi.usage`).
- **Task**: a durable state machine that saves a checkpoint at every step, so a restarted process continues from the last one. The Harness runs answers as built-in tasks: `pi.generation` calls the model, `pi.tool` runs one tool call, and `pi.post-tools` continues once a round's tools are done.
- **Submission**: something you hand to a conversation, either user input or an entry to write, which you can wait for.
- **Turn and run**: a turn is one model response and its tool calls; a run is the turns from an input to its final answer. A conversation is busy while a run is going.
- **Registry**: your tools, system prompt sections, hooks, and tasks. It can change while the Harness runs; new work uses the new state.

One answered input, as entries and tasks:

```text
submit(input) → pi.user
  pi.generation → pi.system (only if the prompt or tools changed), pi.assistant (tool calls)
  pi.tool × n   → pi.tool-result × n
  pi.post-tools
  pi.generation → pi.assistant (answer) → submission done
```

## Persist and Resume

Use SQLite or JSONL storage to keep conversations across restarts:

```typescript
import { openNodeSqliteStorage } from "@earendil-works/pi-durable/storage/sqlite/node";

const harness = await Harness.open(await openNodeSqliteStorage("./session.sqlite"), { models, registry }, context);
const root = await harness.root(context); // the same root as last time
harness.resume(); // continue any run the last process left unfinished
```

Work interrupted by a crash or close stays pending. `resume()` starts the task scheduler; submitting or waiting starts it too. A retried submission with the same `requestId` returns the existing submission instead of submitting twice:

```typescript
const submission = await root.submit({ type: "input", content: "Hello", requestId: "greeting-1" }, context);
// After a restart: the same request ID finds the same submission.
const again = await root.submit({ type: "input", content: "Hello", requestId: "greeting-1" }, context);
// again.id === submission.id
```

`harness.submission(id)` reacquires a submission by ID, for example to wait for it after a restart.

## Tools

26:- [Usage and Cost](#usage-and-cost)
78:- **Document**: typed JSON state stored next to the transcript and changed in commits. Built-in ones hold each conversation's settings (`pi.conversation.config`), the running generation and tools (`pi.live`), queued submissions (`pi.inbox`), and spend (`pi.usage`).
80:- **Submission**: something you hand to a conversation, either user input or an entry to write, which you can wait for.
115:`harness.submission(id)` reacquires a submission by ID, for example to wait for it after a restart.
149:Each call runs as its own durable task. Its intent is committed before `execute()` runs. If the process dies mid-call, the tool reruns on reopen only when it is declared `replay: "safe"`; otherwise the model gets an `interrupted` error result with the output committed so far. Throwing from `execute()` gives the model an error result. A result can also return `usage`, which is added to the conversation's [usage](#usage-and-cost). It can also return `control: { terminate: true }`: when every result of the round asks for it, the run ends without another model request.

> New issues and PRs from new contributors are auto-closed by default. Maintainers review auto-closed issues daily. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). # Pi Agent Harness This is the home of the Pi agent harness project including our self extensible coding agent. * **[@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent](packages/coding-agent)**: Interactive coding agent CLI * **[@earendil-works/pi-agent-core](packages/agent)**: Agent runtime with tool calling and state management * **[@earendil-works/pi-ai](packages/ai)**: Unified multi-provider LLM API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, …) To learn more about Pi: * [Visit pi.dev](https://pi.dev), the project website with demos * [Read the documentation](https://pi.dev/docs/latest), but you can also ask the agent to explain itself ## All Packages | Package | Description | |---------|-------------| | **[@earendil-works/chord](packages/chord)** | Standalone application-composition runtime for services, replicated state, RPC, and plugins | | **[@earendil-works/pi-telemetry](packages/telemetry)** | Vendor-neutral telemetry contracts, reference adapter, conformance tests, and typed schemas | | **[@earendil-works/pi-ai](packages/ai)** | Unified multi-provider LLM API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.) | | **[@earendil-works/pi-durable](packages/durable)** | Durable conversation, task, and document runtime | | **[@earendil-works/pi-agent-core](packages/agent)** | Agent runtime with tool calling and state management | | **[@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent](packages/coding-agent)** | Interactive coding agent CLI | | **[@earendil-works/pi-tui](packages/tui)** | Terminal UI library with differential rendering | For Slack/chat automation and workflows see [earendil-works/pi-chat](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi-chat). ## Permissions & Containerization Pi does not include a built-in permission system for restricting filesystem, process, network, or credential access. By default, it runs with the permissions of the user and process that launched it. If you need stronger boundaries, containerize or sandbox Pi. See [packages/coding-agent/docs/containerization.md](packages/coding-agent/docs/containerization.md) for three patterns: - **Gondolin extension**: keep `pi` and provider auth on the host while routing built-in tools and `!` commands into a local Linux micro-VM. - **Plain Docker**: run the whole `pi` process in a local container for simple isolation. - **OpenShell**: run the whole `pi` process in a policy-controlled sandbox. ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for contribution guidelines and [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for project-specific rules (for both humans and agents). Longer term plans for Pi can also be found in [RFCs](https://rfc.earendil.com/keyword/pi/). ## Development ```bash npm install --ignore-scripts # Install all dependencies without running lifecycle scripts npm run build # Refresh model data, then build all packages npm run build:offline # Rebuild using existing model data without network access npm run check # Lint, format, and type check packages/agent/docs: assistant-durability.md harness.md mobile-handoff pico pico-v3.md pico2.md plugins.md post-wp05-roadmap.md rpc.md runtime-simplification.md telemetry-schema.md telemetry.md tool-durability.md values.md work-packages packages/coding-agent/docs: cli-integration.md cli.md compaction.md configuration.md containerization.md custom-provider.md docs.json environment-variables.md extensions.md how-pi-works.md images index.md json.md keybindings.md llama-cpp.md mcp.md message-types.md models.md packages.md prompt-templates.md providers.md quickstart.md # Changelog ## [Unreleased] ## [0.99.1] - 2026-09-29 ## [0.99.0] - 2026-09-29 ### Added - Added the `onProviderStreamEvent` agent option, which is passed to provider streams to observe parsed provider events before normalization ([#9784](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/9784), [#9901](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/pull/9901) by [@davidbrai](https://github.com/davidbrai)). - The agent loop now records the requested thinking level as `thinkingLevel` on each assistant message. ## [0.87.1] - 2026-09-22 ## [0.87.0] - 2026-09-21 ### Breaking Changes - Removed `AgentOptions.shouldStopAfterTurn` and `AgentLoopConfig.shouldStopAfterTurn`. Use `finishTurn` and return `{ action: "end" }` to stop after the completed turn: ```ts // Before shouldStopAfterTurn: async (turn, signal) => await shouldStop(turn, signal), // After finishTurn: async (turn, signal) => { // shouldStopAfterTurn previously ran only for normal responses. if (turn.message.stopReason === "error" || turn.message.stopReason === "aborted") return; return (await shouldStop(turn, signal)) ? { action: "end" } : undefined; }, ``` `finishTurn` runs after the assistant and all tool results are finalized but before `turn_end`; its decision is applied after `turn_end`. It also runs for error and aborted responses, whose decisions are ignored because those responses remain hard exits. The guard in the migration preserves the old hook's normal-response-only invocation, including avoiding predicate side effects on hard exits. Returning `{ action: "end" }` leaves steering and follow-up queues untouched and skips `prepareNextTurn`. ### Added - Added `prepareRequest`, which runs before every provider request, including the first. For example, return `{ context: { ...context, messages: persistedMessages } }` to install canonical context after already-selected input is emitted without introducing another queue poll. - Added `finishTurn`, which runs after assistant/tool-result finalization and before `turn_end` for normal, error, and aborted responses. Return `{ action: "end" }` to end a normal run after `turn_end`, or `undefined` to preserve normal scheduling. `{ action: "continue" }` ensures one next provider request: existing tool-result, steering, or follow-up scheduling can satisfy that request without adding another one; otherwise the loop makes one context-only request. Error and aborted responses remain hard exits. - Added `Agent.peekQueuedMessages()` to preview the next queue-selected batch without consuming it. ### Fixed - Fixed harness reads misclassifying text files beginning with `GIF` as images ([#9755](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/9755)). ## [0.86.1] - 2026-09-20 ## [0.86.0] - 2026-09-19 ## [0.85.1] - 2026-09-05 ## [0.85.0] - 2026-09-04 ### Fixed - Fixed proxied assistant responses dropping persisted provider-native thinking levels. - Fixed the write tool reporting UTF-16 code-unit counts as byte counts by removing the misleading count ([#8979](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/8979)). ## [0.84.4] - 2026-08-28 ### Breaking Changes - Changed `prepareNextTurn` and `prepareNextTurnWithContext` to run only after `shouldStopAfterTurn` and queued-message checks determine that the agent loop will start another assistant turn. They no longer run after final or terminating turns; move end-of-run work to `agent_end` handling ([#6879](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/6879)). ### Fixed - Fixed Windows `NodeExecutionEnv` aborts crashing when `taskkill.exe` is unavailable on `PATH` ([#6596](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/6596)). ### Removed - Removed the withdrawn manual-drive configuration, action inspection methods, action outcomes, and snapshot action field from `AgentHarness`. ## [0.84.3] - 2026-08-24 ### Fixed - Fixed single-object `edit` tool inputs failing validation by accepting them as one-edit arrays ([#7835](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/7835)). - Fixed root Markdown files such as `README.md` and `AGENTS.md` in skill directories being reported as broken skills unless they declare valid skill frontmatter ([#7805](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/7805)). ## [0.84.2] - 2026-08-14

When Mario Zechner — creator of the libGDX game framework — got frustrated with Claude Code's growing complexity, he built something radically different: an AI coding agent with exactly four tools, a system prompt under 1,000 tokens, and a philosophy that what you leave out matters more than what you put in.

messages.text:
I researched Pi and found it is a good technical fit for a sidecar whose host owns everything; the main risk is how fast its API changes. Details are below with sources. Two basics first: the project has moved to [github.com/earendil-works/pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi), and the npm scope is now `@earendil-works/*`. Mario Zechner [joined Earendil in April 2026](https://mariozechner.at/posts/2026-04-08-ive-sold-out/). The `@mariozechner/*` packages stopped at 0.73.1 on 2026-05-07.

I also ran a local test (Node 26.10, not 24). With my own `streamFn` standing in for an RPC to the host, `Agent` ran a tool-calling turn and a slow async tool. It saved the transcript with `JSON.stringify`, restored it into a new `Agent` and continued. esbuild bundled all of that into one CJS file that ran.

## 1. Package layout
- **Which package does what:** `pi-ai` is the model layer, `pi-agent-core` is the agent loop, `pi-coding-agent` is the CLI. `pi-durable` (crash-safe runs) and `chord` are newer additions ([root README](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/README.md)).
- **Version and license:** 0.99.1, released 2026-09-29. MIT.
- **Node:** requires `>=22.19.0`, so Node 24 is fine.
- **Release pace:** 51 versions since May 2026, roughly weekly. The previous scope had 308 `pi-ai` versions.
- **Module format:** ESM only. The exports map has `import` conditions and no `require`.
- **Dependencies:**
  - `pi-agent-core` has 7 direct: `pi-ai`, `chord`, `pi-telemetry`, `typebox`, `diff`, `ignore`, `yaml`.
  - `pi-ai` has 10 direct, including the full Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and AWS Bedrock SDKs.
  - Installing both gave 118 MB of `node_modules`.
- **esbuild:** `--format=cjs --platform=node` gave a 787 KB file (892 KB with the OpenAI-compatible provider). No warnings, no `import.meta`, and it ran.
- **Not verified:** the full SEA build. My Homebrew Node is dynamically linked and can't host a SEA.
- **Doc mismatch:** the README tells you to import `@earendil-works/pi-ai/models`, but that subpath isn't in the published exports.

## 2. LLM layer (pi-ai)
- **Providers** are built with `createProvider({id, auth, models, api})`, and a `Model` is plain data (id, api, baseUrl, cost, contextWindow) ([pi-ai README](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/ai/README.md#custom-providers)).
- **Custom transport: yes.** The agent requires a `streamFn(model, context, options)` that returns an `AssistantMessageEventStream`. You create one with `createAssistantMessageEventStream()`, push events into it, and pi makes no HTTP calls of its own. I ran this.
- **OpenAI Chat Completions:** `openAICompletionsApi()` takes a configurable `baseUrl`, `headers`, and a custom `fetch`. `OpenAICompletionsCompat` covers quirks such as the max-tokens field name, usage in streams, and the `developer` role.
- **Stream events:** `start`, `text_start/delta/end`, `thinking_start/delta/end`, `toolcall_start/delta/end`, `done`, `error` (source: `types.ts`).
- **Usage:** input, output, cacheRead, cacheWrite, optional reasoning tokens, plus cost figures taken from the model's cost table.
- **Reasoning fields:** it reads `reasoning_content`, `reasoning` and `reasoning_text`, and uses the first non-empty one as `thinking_delta` (`openai-completions.ts` ~L602). `reasoning_details` is kept for replay. Venice has no special handling.

## 3. Agent loop (pi-agent-core)
Source: [agent README](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/agent/README.md).
- **Running a turn:** `new Agent({initialState, streamFn})`, then `prompt()`, `continue()`, `waitForIdle()`. The lower-level `agentLoop` / `agentLoopContinue` are async generators.
- **You own persistence.** `state.messages` is plain JSON that you set and read. `prepareRequest` can swap in your stored context before every model request.
- **Different from the OpenAI SDK:** the system prompt and tool declarations live inside the transcript as `system` messages.
- **Tools:** schemas are TypeBox. A plain JSON Schema object also worked in my test, but arguments get validated and coerced (a number became accepted for a string field). Issue [#7607](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/7607), asking to switch validation off for host-validated tools, is open.
- **Tool execution:** `execute(id, params, signal, onUpdate)` is any async function, so a long RPC is fine. Tools run in parallel by default, or sequentially if set globally or per tool.
- **Cancellation:** `agent.abort()`, and an AbortSignal is passed to `streamFn`, the tools and the hooks.
- **Events:** `agent_start/end`, `turn_start/end`, `message_start/update/end`, `tool_execution_start/update/end`.
- **Mid-run messages:** `steer()` and `followUp()` queues are supported.
- **Human approval:** only in-process. `beforeToolCall` can block a call, or wait on the host before returning. There is no built-in "suspend and resume after a restart" in agent-core. You would store the transcript ending in the tool call, then append the tool result and call `continue()` yourself.
  - `pi-durable` does resume after a crash, but it is marked "Experimental. The API changes without notice" and owns its own storage ([durable README](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/durable/README.md)).
  - The `deferred` stop reason is for delayed provider responses, not approvals.
- **Compaction:** helpers are exported (`compact`, `shouldCompact`, `generateSummary`). They call models through a pi-ai registry, and `generateSummaryWithRequest` takes a request function, so compaction could plausibly go through the host (not verified). Open bugs: [#9602](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/9602), [#10092](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/10092).
- **Usage** is reported per assistant message.

## 4. Maturity and risk
- **Adoption:** 110,379 stars, 14,039 forks, about 287 contributors, 236 open issues. Last week `pi-ai` had about 6.57M downloads and `pi-agent-core` about 5.06M. It is the engine behind OpenClaw ([OpenClaw docs](https://openclawlab.com/en/docs/pi/)).
- **Breaking changes:** the agent-core changelog has 12 "Breaking Changes" sections, 10 of them since 0.65. For example, 0.87.0 removed `shouldStopAfterTurn` and 0.84.4 changed when `prepareNextTurn` runs. pi-ai has 25 such sections ([CHANGELOG](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/agent/CHANGELOG.md)).
- **Stability:** still pre-1.0, with no statement that the API is stable. Parts are explicitly experimental (`experimental/pico3`, chord services, pi-durable).
- **Docs:** detailed READMEs, but the harness docs read like internal design notes.
- **Contributions:** new contributors' issues and PRs are closed automatically, then reviewed daily.

## 5. Fit for a sidecar where Rust owns everything
- The main risk is API churn and a deep version pin. Plan on adapter tests at every upgrade.
- You must build fake `Model` objects (api, provider, cost, window), and pass zero costs if billing happens elsewhere.
- Stored sessions need migrating to Pi's `AgentMessage` format, with the system prompt inside the transcript.
- Install weight: provider SDKs are always installed even though tree-shaking keeps them out of the bundle.
- The root export also brings coding-harness code (bash/read/edit tools, a Node environment). It is tree-shaken out, but it adds surface area.
- Crash-safe approvals would mean either writing your own or adopting experimental `pi-durable`, which wants to own storage.
- A tool whose arguments fail TypeBox validation or coercion is never run, which could clash with host-side validation ([#7607](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/7607)).
- Issue [#9787](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/9787) (a global `undici` dispatcher that breaks `fetch` in embedded hosts) is open, but I found no `setGlobalDispatcher` in the pi-ai or agent-core builds. It appears limited to the coding-agent package.

**Could not verify:** a SEA build on Node 24, custom storage backends for `pi-durable`, and routing compaction entirely through the host.

The test files are in `/tmp/pitest` (`app.mjs`, `out.cjs`) and the cloned repo is in `/tmp/pi`. Nothing in the Clovy repo was changed.

Dá para trocar para o Pi. A arquitetura ajuda: o motor fica atrás de uma interface pequena, `AgentEngine` ([`types.ts:213`](agent-runtime/src/types.ts)), e o Rust, o protocolo stdio e o React não precisam mudar. O trabalho fica quase todo em 2 arquivos do sidecar e nos testes dele. A única parte difícil é a pausa para aprovação, que o Pi não tem pronta.

## Situação atual do Pi (29/09/2026)

- **Pacotes:** o projeto mudou para [`earendil-works/pi`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) e os pacotes agora são `@earendil-works/pi-ai` (camada de modelos) e `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core` (o loop). O escopo antigo `@mariozechner/*` parou na 0.73.1.
- **Maturidade:** versão 0.99.1, licença MIT, pré-1.0, com releases quase semanais. O changelog do `agent-core` tem 12 seções de "Breaking Changes", 10 delas desde a 0.65.
- **Adoção:** cerca de 110 mil estrelas e 5 milhões de downloads por semana; é o motor do OpenClaw.
- **Teste local do agente de pesquisa:** com um transporte próprio no lugar da rede, o agente rodou um turno com ferramentas, salvou e restaurou o histórico, e o esbuild gerou um único arquivo CJS de cerca de 890 KB que funcionou. O executável único (SEA) em Node 24 não foi testado.

## O que usamos do Agents SDK hoje e o equivalente no Pi

| Uso atual ([`sdk-engine.ts`](agent-runtime/src/sdk-engine.ts)) | No Pi | Esforço |
|---|---|---|
| Modelo via RPC: um cliente OpenAI falso dentro do `OpenAIChatCompletionsModel` | `streamFn` próprio, ou o provider de Chat Completions com `fetch` customizado que manda cada chamada ao Rust. O Pi já lê `reasoning_content`/`reasoning` (o caso da Venice) | Baixo a médio |
| Steering: hoje é um improviso que injeta a mensagem no próximo request | `agent.steer()` e `followUp()` nativos | Fica **melhor** |
| Ferramentas com JSON Schema vindo do Rust | O Pi espera TypeBox; JSON Schema cru funcionou, mas o Pi valida e **converte** argumentos (um número passou como string). A issue [#7607](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/7607) está aberta | Médio, com risco |
| `needsApproval`, com o `RunState.toString()/fromString()` salvo no SQLite para retomar depois da aprovação, mesmo após reiniciar o app | **Não existe.** Só dá para bloquear dentro do processo (`beforeToolCall`). O `pi-durable` é experimental e quer controlar o próprio armazenamento | **Alto**: implementar nós mesmos |
| Clarificação e pedido de segredo, que usam essa mesma pausa | Vêm juntos com a pausa acima | Incluído acima |
| Guardrail de pré-aprovação do Notion | Chamada no `beforeToolCall` antes de pausar | Baixo |
| Falha do host encerra o run, mas erro de argumento volta ao modelo (`errorFunction`) | Precisa verificar como o Pi trata exceção no `execute` | Médio |
| `maxTurns: 40` e no máximo 4 ferramentas em paralelo | Contador em `turn_end` e um semáforo nosso | Baixo |
| Compactação via `getStreamedResponse` | Chamada direta ao `streamFn` | Baixo |
| Uso de tokens | Vem por mensagem; é só somar | Baixo |

### Como resolver a pausa para aprovação

1. Quando o modelo pedir uma ferramenta que exige aprovação, encerra-se o run nesse ponto.
2. O histórico do Pi (`state.messages`, que é JSON puro), terminando no tool call pendente, é salvo no `serializedState` que o Rust já guarda.
3. No `run.resume`, o engine executa a ferramenta aprovada no host (ou monta a resposta de recusa), acrescenta o resultado e chama `agent.continue()`.

É o mesmo contrato que o Rust já usa, então nada muda do lado dele.

## Impacto fora do sidecar

- **Rust:** quase nenhum. Ele guarda os itens no próprio formato tipado e só monta o formato do SDK ao enviar o histórico ([`api.rs:2310`](src-tauri/src/agent_runtime/api.rs)). Converter isso para mensagens do Pi fica no TypeScript.
- **Frontend e protocolo:** nenhuma mudança.
- **Runs parados esperando aprovação na hora da atualização:** o estado deles está no formato do SDK antigo e o Pi não consegue retomá-los. É preciso expirá-los com uma mensagem ou fazer um conversor único.
- **Regras do repo:**
  - Um ADR novo substituindo o 0038 só na escolha do SDK; a arquitetura continua a mesma.
  - Fixar uma versão exata do Pi com pelo menos 7 dias, pela regra de cooldown: a 0.99.1 saiu hoje.
  - Instalar pelo `sfw`.

## Ganhos e custos reais

**Ganhos:**
- Steering e follow-up nativos.
- O loop fica mais simples e mais nosso.
- Eventos de raciocínio e de ferramentas mais ricos.
- Sai a dependência nominal da OpenAI.

**Custos:**
- A pausa e retomada de aprovação precisa ser construída por nós.
- A API do Pi muda muito: cada atualização exige testes de adaptação.
- Aparece a questão da validação e coerção de argumentos.
- O ganho em providers é pequeno aqui: toda chamada de modelo passa pela Clovy API em formato Chat Completions, então o suporte do Pi a Anthropic, Google e outros não é aproveitado. Para aproveitar, a Clovy API também teria que expor esses formatos.

**Estimativa:**
- **Reescrita do sidecar:** cerca de 1,1 mil linhas, somando o `sdk-engine.ts` e o `rpc-model-provider.ts`.
- **Testes:** portar os de `agent-runtime/test/`.
- **Tempo:** mais ou menos 1 a 2 semanas de trabalho focado, com a pausa de aprovação e os testes de regressão das ferramentas como maior parte.

## Recomendação

Antes do ADR, fazer um spike curto de 2 a 3 dias numa branch: um `PiEngine` que implementa a mesma interface `AgentEngine`, cobrindo três pontos:
1. **Modelo pela Clovy API com streaming e raciocínio**, rodando os testes de ferramenta atuais (`sdk-tool-loop.test.ts`).
2. **Aprovação:** pausar, reiniciar o processo e retomar (`secret-interruption.test.ts`, `clarification.test.ts`).
3. **Build:** gerar o executável único em Node 24.

Se os três passarem, a troca é segura e o ADR se escreve com dados. Se a pausa ou o SEA travarem, o custo real aparece antes de a gente se comprometer.

Qual é a principal motivação para trocar: steering, usar outros formatos de provider, ecossistema, ou tirar a dependência da OpenAI? Isso muda o peso dos custos acima. Se quiser, já começo o spike numa branch.

- **Pacotes:** o projeto mudou para [`earendil-works/pi`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) e os pacotes agora são `@earendil-works/pi-ai` (camada de modelos) e `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core` (o loop). O escopo antigo `@mariozechner/*` parou na 0.73.1.

messages.text:
Sim, o Pi tem aprovação. No `pi-agent-core` existe o hook `beforeToolCall`, e o `pi-coding-agent` traz uma extensão de exemplo, a [`permission-gate.ts`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/permission-gate.ts). Na minha análise anterior eu exagerei quando marquei esse ponto como "alto".

## A diferença entre os dois modelos

**Como o Pi aprova: "pausa em memória".** O loop chega na ferramenta, chama `beforeToolCall`, e esse hook fica esperando uma resposta (`await ctx.ui.select("Allow?")`). O agente continua vivo, parado dentro de uma Promise, até alguém responder. Isso funciona bem num CLI em que você está na frente do terminal.

**Como o Clovy aprova hoje: "para e salva".** Quando o modelo pede uma ferramenta que exige aprovação, o run **termina** com status `waiting_for_user` e o estado vai para o SQLite ([`host.rs:957`](src-tauri/src/agent_runtime/host.rs)). Quando você aprova, um run novo começa a partir desse estado salvo.

Esse modelo existe por causa de casos que o Clovy tem e um CLI não tem:
- **Rotinas agendadas.** Uma rotina roda às 3h da manhã sem ninguém olhando e para numa aprovação (`routines::mark_agent_run_waiting`). Você só aprova às 10h. Nesse intervalo o app pode ter fechado, atualizado sozinho ou o Mac pode ter dormido.
- **Aprovar de outro lugar.** O pedido aparece no HUD, na barra de menus e no celular pareado. Pode levar horas.
- **Queda do sidecar.** Se o processo Node reiniciar, uma Promise em memória some junto, e o pedido de aprovação some com ela.

Em resumo: com a pausa em memória, a aprovação só sobrevive enquanto o processo estiver vivo. O Clovy precisa que ela sobreviva a fechar o app.

## O que eu sugiro de fato (mais simples do que parecia)

Usar a aprovação nativa do Pi no caso normal, mais uma recuperação para quando o processo morre:

1. **Caso normal:** o `beforeToolCall` avisa o Rust ("preciso de aprovação") e fica esperando. Quando você aprova, o Rust manda a resposta, a Promise resolve e o loop do Pi continua sozinho. É a aprovação do Pi, sem gambiarra.
2. **Caso o processo morra no meio:** aqui o Pi ajuda. O estado dele é só a lista de mensagens em JSON (`state.messages`), que já salvamos. Ao reabrir, o Rust recria o agente com essas mensagens, que terminam no pedido de ferramenta pendente. Quando você aprova, executamos a ferramenta, acrescentamos o resultado e chamamos `agent.continue()`.

O passo 2 é a parte que eu tinha chamado de "construir nós mesmos", mas são umas 100 a 150 linhas. Com o Agents SDK atual isso é até pior: o estado dele é um blob opaco (`RunState.toString()`) que só o próprio SDK consegue ler.

## Se você não precisar desses casos

Se estiver tudo bem perder uma aprovação pendente quando o app fecha, dá para usar só o passo 1. São umas 50 linhas, e na queda o run fica como "interrompido, tente de novo". O custo cai quase todo nas rotinas agendadas, que acabariam falhando em vez de esperar você.

Minha recomendação é fazer os dois passos. O passo 1 é a aprovação do Pi mesmo, e o passo 2 é uma rede de segurança barata justamente porque o estado do Pi é JSON simples.
